prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought many-atom optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the strongest combination on the shortlist of a new measurement capability, independent reproduction and demonstrated downstream use. The magic-wavelength trap removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel, which is what allows 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and instability averaging down in hours instead of weeks. JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and others have built clocks that agree with each other at that level, and they are already used for centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and the roadmap to a redefinition of the second. Five of eight members ranked B045 and all five proposed the same two names, so the attribution is as clean as any candidate on the list. The measurement basis for much of what we call progress in physics is how well we can measure, and this is the clearest case where a concept (Katori's magic wavelength) was turned by careful experiment (Ye's group, and Katori's own) into an instrument that changed what can be observed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from earlier prizes: the 2005 award (Hall, Hansch) covered the frequency comb and the laser stabilization that clocks depend on, and 2012 (Wineland) covered single-ion control and optical clocks. A reader could call lattice clocks a refinement of that line. I do not think that holds, since the lattice clock addresses the quantum-projection-noise and Doppler limits in a different way, but it is a real argument. A second concern is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still prospective, and contributions by Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE group, and Hall and Hansch via laser stabilization, fall outside two names.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B008, quantum control of mechanical motion, first as a conceptually clean fundamental advance on the boundary between the quantum and the everyday world, and puts B045 second.
responses.response: I agree B008 is physically interesting and I ranked it last of my list only because of attribution, not scientific disinterest. My reservation is that the first ground-state results were near-simultaneous across Cleland, Teufel, Painter and others, and as you note yourself any three of five leaves out a major contributor. A prize where the experimental priority is that unsettled risks being arbitrary. Quantum-limited readout in optomechanics is measurement-relevant, but its practical reach (transduction, sensing) is still developing, whereas for B045 comparison between independent clocks is already routine. If you can show a clean decisive trio I would reconsider, but I would not place it above a two-name prize with five-member support.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors, a clean demonstration of quantum optics in a solid-state circuit, while flagging the 2025 prize overlap and his own possible conflict.
responses.response: I ranked B026 second and share the scientific assessment: strong coupling of one artificial atom to one photon, with dispersive readout, is a lasting idea. Where I differ is on timing and the interaction with the 2025 award. Clarke, Devoret and Martinis were recognised for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, and Devoret and Schoelkopf are close scientific neighbours, so a cQED prize one year later invites the argument that the committee is staying in one corner of quantum hardware. The attribution (Girvin, Huang) is also not clean. I would keep B026 as my first alternative, but I think B045 is the better choice this year because it carries no such overlap and your own flagged connection to this community would be a further complication.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube's high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first as a detector-driven opening of a new window with careful background rejection, and B045 second.
responses.response: I share your valuing of calibration and background control and I think B016 is a serious candidate, which is why I would not wave it away. My concern is the one you raise yourself: the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) rest largely on a single experiment, and a two-name credit for a collaboration-scale detector with AMANDA predecessors is contestable on hardware versus analysis. B045 has the comparison between independent laboratories built in as its confirmation, which gives me more confidence about reproducibility. I would be glad to see the credit question for B016 settled by someone with more astroparticle background than I have.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a simple, general mechanism that has reshaped the classification of phases, with recognition overdue rather than premature, but notes the supplied names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: I accept that the scientific weight of B040 is large and that stability over fifteen years speaks for maturity. My difficulty is exactly the attribution problem you identify: the HgTe experiment followed the BHZ proposal, Mele is a co-originator whom a three-person cap excludes, Hasan's 3D spectroscopy is a separate step, and one of the key theorists is deceased. As an experimentalist I am also wary of ranking it above a candidate where two names are agreed by every member who ranked it. If the committee can fix the credit I would raise it in my ordering, but I cannot support it as the preferred configuration on the current record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether a two-name credit appropriately leaves out Takamoto, Lemonde and others who demonstrated early strontium lattice clocks, and how the Katori proposal priority is judged.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, which would strengthen the practical case but is not required for the physics.
If B026 or B040 were to become the committee's leading candidate, whether their attribution problems can be resolved within three names.
statement.conflict_note: Possible but mild connection: I spent a year during my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's work on laser stabilization and the comb underlies the clock field and is connected to Jun Ye's group at JILA. I have no direct collaboration or supervisory relation with Katori or Ye that I know of, and this is not disqualifying, but the committee should be aware. Separately, my work on rare-earth-ion quantum memories and my WACQT role overlap with the quantum-information candidates (B007, B026, B028) and with Chalmers, where Göran Johansson works.
